extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, creative writers, translators, artists, and patrons interested in taste, criticism, and moral instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Producing and judging short periodical essays, translations of classical poetry, and art criticism in the manner of The Spectator — aiming at moral instruction, tasteful persuasion, and faithful rendering of originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of Perfection in Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: This Ode ... was preserved by an eminent Greek Critick, who inserted it intire in his Works, as a Pattern of Perfection in the Structure of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat exemplary classical pieces as models of structural perfection; when translating or imitating, attend closely to the original's structural virtues rather than paraphrasing freely. The critic preserved the piece whole because its structure served as a pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing unnatural witticisms in translations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Compositions of the Ancients, which have not in them any of those unnatural Witticisms that are the Delight of ordinary Readers, are extremely difficult to render into another Tongue, so as the Beauties of the Original may not appear weak and faded in the Translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not add modern 'witticisms' or fashionable conceits when translating ancient works; such insertions tend to obscure or weaken the original beauties. Aim for fidelity of tone and effect rather than clever modern turns of phrase that please casual readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the beauties and force of the original in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translators should render the Beauties of the Original so that they do not appear weak and faded in the Translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize conveying the original's compelling images, emotional force, and formal qualities. Beware of literalism that loses poetic force and of freer renderings that domesticate and flatten the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize authenticity and anachronisms before publishing ancient texts
rubrics_metrics.description: As there seem to be in it some Anachronisms and Deviations from the ancient Orthography, I am not wholly satisfied myself that it is authentick, and not rather the Production of one of those Grecian Sophisters, who have imposed upon the World several spurious Works of this Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing or translating purported ancient manuscripts, check for anachronisms, orthographic inconsistencies, and other signs of spuriousness; exercise caution in asserting authenticity and be transparent about doubts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use painting (and visual art) to improve manners and instruct
rubrics_metrics.description: The Art of Painting is made so little Use of to the Improvement of our Manners ... If the Virtues and Vices ... were given us by the Painter in the Characters of real Life, and the Persons of Men and Women whose Actions have rendered them laudable or infamous; we should not see a good History-Piece without receiving an instructive Lecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer history-pieces and depictions of real human virtue or vice over decorative/mythological subjects when the goal is moral instruction. Paintings that represent moral actions in lifelike, affecting ways can convey lessons more immediately than written texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey passion and character through features and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Painter ... not only express the Passion or Concern as it sits upon him who is drawn, but has under those Features the Height of the Painters Imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In both painting and descriptive writing, render emotions and character through concrete, arranged detail — facial expression, posture, group composition — so that the viewer/reader feels the passions rather than merely being told them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects that inspire noble sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible ... to be unmoved at the Horror and Reverence which appear in the whole Assembly when the mercenary Man fell down dead ... Present Authority, late Suffering, Humility and Majesty, Despotick Command, and Divine Love, are at once seated in his celestial Aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select scenes and subjects that naturally evoke admiration, pity, reverence, and other noble sentiments; carefully stage the elements (authority, suffering, humility, etc.) so the work generates moral feeling and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize modesty and diffidence as signs of merit in artists
rubrics_metrics.description: It is certainly the greatest Honour we can do our Country, to distinguish Strangers of Merit who apply to us with Modesty and Diffidence ... a modest Behaviour should alarm us to examine whether we do not lose something excellent under that Disadvantage in the Possessor of that Quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating unfamiliar artists or authors, treat modesty and diffidence as possible indicators of genuine merit rather than reasons to ignore them; look beyond self-promotion when curating or patronizing talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reproduction/publication to broaden access to great works
rubrics_metrics.description: As an Engraver is to the Painter what a Printer is to an Author ... it is worthy Her Majesty's Name, that she has encouraged that Noble Artist ... to publish these Works of Raphael.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support and use affordable reproductions (engravings, prints, printed editions) to make exemplary works accessible to a wider public; dissemination aids moral and aesthetic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion in speech and writing: pick and cull thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: The great Difference is that the first knows how to pick and cull his Thoughts for Conversation, by suppressing some, and communicating others; whereas the other lets them all indifferently fly out in Words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good writer or conversationalist practices discretion: edit which thoughts to express, order them for effect, and suppress irrelevant or injurious remarks. In private intimacy different rules apply (thinking aloud), but public composition demands selection and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion makes other talents useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Without it Learning is Pedantry, and Wit Impertinence; Virtue itself looks like Weakness; the best Parts only qualify a Man to be more sprightly in Errors, and active to his own Prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value editorial judgment and prudential taste: the capacity to apply knowledge, wit, and virtue appropriately is what makes them effective. In editing or composing, use discretion to direct talents to proper ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish discretion from cunning
rubrics_metrics.description: Discretion points out the noblest Ends to us, and pursues the most proper and laudable Methods of attaining them: Cunning has only private selfish Aims, and sticks at nothing which may make them succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for sane, long-view prudence (discretion) rather than calculating, short-sighted manipulation (cunning). In character portrayals and moral argument, make the distinction clear: discretion is public-spirited and methodical; cunning is petty and opportunistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think forward: consider distant and moral consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cast of Mind which is natural to a discreet Man, makes him look forward into Futurity, and consider what will be his Condition Millions of Ages hence, as well as what it is at present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose and evaluate actions, policies, and artistic choices with awareness of long-term moral consequences, not merely immediate gain. In rhetoric and narrative, foreground consequences to encourage prudential judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ridicule and satire to counter excessive passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule, perhaps, is a better Expedient against Love than sober Advice, and I am of Opinion, that Hudibras and Don Quixote may be as effectual to cure the Extravagancies of this Passion, as any of the old Philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire and comic ridicule can be effective tools to check extravagant passions or follies in readers; consider using humorous exposure rather than purely didactic instruction when aiming to correct social or personal excesses.
